nameStory: This spider gets its name from Mabel, though the exact identity of this namesake has been lost to scientific history. The "orchard" part of the name refers to its habit of building webs in fruit trees and garden areas, where it's often spotted spinning its delicate nets among apple and pear branches.
description: Mabel's Orchard Orbweaver is a small, delicate spider that builds classic circular webs in gardens and wooded areas. Like other long-jawed orbweavers, it has notably elongated mouthparts (chelicerae) that extend forward from its head. This species is quite rare in New England, with only a single confirmed observation in the region. It typically measures less than half an inch in body length, with a somewhat flattened appearance when viewed from above.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated abdomen with a somewhat flattened profile, and distinctively long, forward-projecting jaws that look almost like tiny tusks

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Classic circular orb web, usually built at an angle rather than perfectly vertical, with sticky spiral threads that feel tacky to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider with body length typically under 0.4 inches, legs span roughly the size of a quarter when extended

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often hangs head-down in the center of its web during the day, quickly vibrating the web when disturbed

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in two rows, though they appear quite small relative to the prominent jaws

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, found primarily in the southernmost areas of the region in mixed deciduous forests and garden edges. When present, it favors areas with fruit trees, woodland borders, and shrubby understory where it can string its webs between branches about 3-6 feet off the ground.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin appearing in late spring as temperatures warm, starting to build their first webs of the season among new foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found building webs and hunting. Look for fresh, intact orb webs in early morning.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active through early fall, with mating likely occurring during this period before winter arrives.
seasonality.winter: Not active during winter months in New England; likely overwinters as eggs or juveniles in protected locations.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that there's only been one confirmed sighting in the entire region - making it one of the most elusive arachnids you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, the Orchard Orbweaver (Leucauge venusta), which is much more common in New England. The key difference is in subtle body proportions and web placement preferences, though distinguishing them often requires expert examination.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England suggests it may be at the very northern edge of its range, with most populations concentrated much further south. Climate change may potentially affect its future distribution in the region.
compareHints: Mabel's Orchard Orbweaver is incredibly similar to the much more common Orchard Orbweaver (Leucauge venusta) found throughout New England. Both share the characteristic long jaws and orb web construction, but Mabel's tends to be slightly smaller and has subtly different markings. Given the rarity of Mabel's species, any long-jawed orbweaver you find in New England is far more likely to be the common Orchard Orbweaver.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The orchard orbweaver can be distinguished from its close relative, the Mabel orchard orbweaver, primarily by geographic range and subtle differences in the abdominal spot patterns.
